SETU: Reverse Learning with a Rule-Governed AI Classmate
for Hindi-Speaking Learners of Telugu

Madhav Malhotra2026900003
Kushal Karan2025204010
Faviana Noronha2025900018
Shaik Areesh2026909008
International Institute of Information Technology, Hyderabad · Language Models and Agents, Monsoon 2026 · Team Token Guessers
Code, data and every result file: https://github.com/MadhavM99/setu-tutor

Abstract

SETU is a tutor for Hindi speakers learning Telugu. At its sentence stage the learner corrects Raju, an AI classmate who makes the mistakes a Hindi speaker makes. Raju's knowledge is stored as data, and the system follows one rule: language models may write text, but ordinary code decides what is shown, how an answer is marked and what the learner's record says. We report what this design achieved and where it fell short. On our test cases no model output reached a learner unchecked and none changed a mark (17 of 17 tool attacks refused; 11 injected messages, no unsafe attempt). We compared five model capabilities with simpler baselines on small frozen case sets using one hosted model. Letting the model call a checking tool raised the share of valid Raju sentences from 0.69 to 0.97, but a controlled re-run shows a fixed loop that simply shows the model its own rejected draft reaches 0.92 against 0.94 at about one fifth of the tokens. Stepwise reasoning, retrieval for hints and separate agent roles did not improve accuracy, and fine-tuning stopped at a data check. The rule-based checker never accepted a wrong answer on held-out cases but agrees poorly with a native speaker's labels (κ = 0.15 against 0.46 for a prompt-only model judge). No learner has used SETU: learner outcomes are simulated, the two simulators order the teaching conditions differently, and the one built on the app's own memory model puts reverse learning last. We state which claims the evidence supports and which remain open.

1 Introduction

Hindi and Telugu belong to different language families, yet they share many Sanskrit-derived words and their scripts correspond almost letter for letter. A Hindi speaker therefore starts with real advantages, and also with habits that cause errors: the question word क्या at the start of a yes/no question, a separate negative word before the verb, the copula है where Telugu uses none. General language apps do not target these habits.

SETU tests one teaching idea, which we call reverse learning: instead of only answering questions, the learner finds and fixes the mistakes of a classmate, Raju. Each of Raju's sentences carries one mistake on a rule the learner has already shown they know. A correct fix "teaches" Raju the rule; if the learner is predicted to have forgotten it, Raju forgets it too and makes the mistake again.

Building such a classmate with a language model raises a control problem. A model asked to act as a weak student knows too much: it writes correct forms, uses words the learner has not met, or drifts into explaining. A model that also marks answers can be talked into a wrong mark. SETU's response is an architecture rule, models write, rules decide: a model may propose a sentence, a hint or a choice among approved lines; deterministic code (code with no model in it, so the same input always gives the same result) decides whether the proposal is shown, marks every answer, and is the only thing that can change the learner's record.

Research questions

The project began with four questions about learners (does correcting a peer improve delayed recall; do predicted errors match real ones; do effects differ by direction; is the checker reliable). Three need human participants we did not have. We therefore separate what our evidence can answer from what it cannot:

  • RQ1 Control. Can any model output reach a learner, or change a mark or the learner's record, without passing a deterministic check? Answerable: attack sets, permission tests.
  • RQ2 Capabilities. Which model capabilities (tool calling, stepwise reasoning, retrieval, a tuned small model, separate roles) improve the classmate's sentence, the coach's hint or the diagnosis of an answer over a simpler baseline? Answerable on small frozen sets.
  • RQ3 Checker. How well does the rule-based checker agree with a native speaker, compared with a prompt-only model judge? Answerable for one labeller and 50 answers.
  • RQ4 Learning. Does correcting Raju improve delayed recall over the same content without him, or over an ordinary tutor? Not answerable here: simulation only.

Contributions

  1. A working tutor in which model roles are proposal-only and a single writer, backed by database permissions, owns learner state (Section 5).
  2. A measured comparison of five model capabilities against baselines, with a controlled ablation that separates the effect of model-chosen tool calls from the effect of conversation memory (Sections 6, 7).
  3. A comparison of a rule-based checker and a model judge against native-speaker labels, reported with its failure (Section 8).
  4. Two learner simulators that disagree, with an analysis of which assumptions the disagreement comes from (Section 8).

The first is an engineering contribution. The second to fourth are empirical findings on small samples; several are negative.

2 Literature Review

Learning by teaching. Students work harder for an agent they believe they are teaching, the protégé effect (Chase et al., 2009), and teachable-agent systems such as Betty's Brain build on it (Biswas et al., 2005). Jin et al. (2024) used a language model as a teachable agent for programming and reported that it tends to know too much. Who benefits is an open question in peer tutoring too: a randomised trial was run specifically to compare the gains of tutors and tutees (Thurston et al., 2021).

Learning from errors. Studying incorrect examples can help when learners explain the error (Große and Renkl, 2007), and taking a test strengthens memory more than rereading (Roediger and Karpicke, 2006). A recent meta-analysis of 42 papers finds only a weak average benefit of erroneous examples (g = 0.136), larger when an explanation activity is included (Alemdag et al., 2025). Reverse learning is thus a hypothesis, not an established effect.

Simulated students. Markel et al. (2023) trained teaching assistants with model-played students. Yuan et al. (2026) name the central problem the competence paradox: a broadly capable model is asked to imitate a learner who knows only part of the material, and argue for an explicit specification of what the simulated learner knows. SETU's classmate state table is one concrete form of such a specification.

Tools, retrieval, and control of agents. ReAct interleaves model reasoning with tool calls (Yao et al., 2023), and retrieval-augmented generation supplies retrieved text to the model (Lewis et al., 2020). Instructions hidden in the data a model reads can redirect it (Greshake et al., 2023). Debenedetti et al. (2025) defend against this by design, keeping untrusted data from steering control flow. SETU applies the same principle in a simpler setting: models have no write tools at all.

Tutoring systems and memory. Knowledge tracing estimates what a learner knows from their answers (Corbett and Anderson, 1995). Spaced repetition schedules reviews from a memory model (Settles and Meeder, 2016); FSRS, which we use, optimises review timing from a difficulty-stability-retrievability model (Ye et al., 2022).

Hindi and Telugu. Contrastive analysis, predicting learner errors from differences between languages, has long been criticised for weak prediction (Wardhaugh, 1970), although typology can predict error distributions in aggregate (Berzak et al., 2015). Resources exist for Indian languages as written by fluent users, including transliteration data (Madhani et al., 2023), language models (Doddapaneni et al., 2023) and a 2025 grammatical-error-correction shared task covering Hindi and Telugu (Bhattacharyya et al., 2025). We found no corpus of errors made by Hindi speakers learning Telugu, so each predicted error in our bank is a hypothesis.

Error bank. Each rule records one contrast (for example: Hindi marks a yes/no question with क्या at the start, Telugu with a suffix at the end) and each item gives a Hindi meaning, the correct Telugu sentence and the wrong sentence a Hindi speaker is predicted to write. The bank marks every rule validity: uncertain and learner_evidence: predicted. An earlier version of this paper reported a first review (24 of 25 rules judged realistic) and a blind marking of 145 answers; the 145-row sheet in this repository carries no labels, so those figures cannot be reproduced from it and we do not rely on them.

Limits of the evaluation sets. The planting cases are the bank's own items, so a method is scored on reproducing sentences the team wrote. In these cases the list of words the model may use contains only the words of the right and the wrong sentence; in the app the list is every word the learner has seen, which is a harder setting. The planned external corpora (IndicCorp, IndicGEC) were not used.

4 Methodology

4.1 System

SETU is a web application (FastAPI, server-rendered Hindi pages, PostgreSQL 16). Learners move up six levels: letters, syllables, words, phrases, sentence rules, and short scenes. A skill counts as learned after three unaided correct answers across two items, two task types and two days. Raju appears at the sentence-rule level once three rules are ready.

One exchange. The planner picks a rule the learner knows and Raju does not, and an item. Raju's sentence is shown. The learner either confirms it or types a correction. The normaliser cleans the answer (for example, Telugu typed with Devanagari letters is converted). The checker compares it with the item's accepted forms and returns one of four verdicts: correct, partial, wrong, or unsure. After a first miss the coach gives one hint; after a second the answer is shown and the learner copies it, which never counts as evidence. A verdict of unsure changes nothing and goes to a teacher's queue. Only an unaided, typed, correct fix teaches Raju the rule.

Who may write. The checker issues verdict objects that other code cannot construct. One component, the OutcomeWriter, accepts only those, a teacher decision signed with a server key, or a forgetting decision from the scheduler. It runs under a restricted database role, and a trigger re-checks each change to Raju's knowledge. Every change is appended to a hash-chained log.

Model roles. Raju writes one sentence; the coach writes one Hindi hint; the Telugu friend in scenes picks among approved lines. Each output passes a filter or is replaced by approved text. For Raju the filter requires exactly the planned mistake, no word the learner has not seen, one sentence in Telugu script and a student's voice. For 43 of 49 items "exactly the planned mistake" means the bank's wrong sentence, since a paraphrase cannot be verified without a person.

4.2 Methods compared

All model runs use one hosted model, gemini-3.5-flash, through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, reasoning effort off, temperature 0.4 for generation and 0 for grading and diagnosis. Each method is scored on the same frozen cases as its baseline.

  • Generation. Prompt only (one draft); resample (up to three independent drafts); harness feedback (the app's loop when these runs were made: the program runs the filter and returns its reason codes); model-chosen tools (the model is told about three read-only checking tools and decides when to call one, at most six model calls).
  • Tool calling. The same generation task scored for tool use, plus two attack sets: 17 model replies that try an unknown or malformed tool call, replayed into the tool handler, and 11 learner-style messages injected into Raju's task.
  • Stepwise reasoning. Diagnose a learner's correction (which word is wrong, which rule, which error type) in three separate steps with or without a self-check step, against one direct call.
  • Retrieval (RAG). BM25 over character n-grams of the 25 rule documents returns three rules for the coach; baselines are no retrieval, the rule title given, and the correct rule given (an upper bound).
  • Fine-tuning. A bar was fixed before generating data: at least 200 validated training pairs covering 12 of 14 rules. Untuned Gemma-3-1B-it was compared with the prompted hosted model.
  • Role separation. Separate Raju and coach calls with the rule-based checker, against one model that writes the sentence and hint and also grades.
  • Checker. The checker and a prompt-only model judge against 50 native-speaker labels.

4.3 Metrics and statistics

Valid rate: share of cases in which a model sentence passed the filter. Leak rate: share in which a draft was the correct sentence. Usable hint: a model hint passed the filter and does not refer to a numbered rule list the learner cannot see. Cohen's κ: agreement beyond chance, κ = (po − pe)/(1 − pe), where po is observed agreement and pe the agreement expected from the label frequencies. False acceptance: answers a native speaker did not mark correct that the system marked correct. False rejection: answers marked correct by the native speaker that the system did not. Proportions carry Wilson 95% intervals. Methods run on the same cases are compared with the exact McNemar test on discordant pairs. With 29 cases only large differences can be detected, and a non-significant difference is never read as equivalence. We do not report a money cost, because no price is recorded in the repository; we report calls and tokens.

5 Experiment Runs

Software checks. 1,309 automated tests pass against PostgreSQL 16 with no model configured; 484 of them are one parametrised test over the frozen cases, so the count is not a measure of coverage. On the 185 held-out cases the checker caught every wrong answer and rejected no correct one, the filters passed every clean Raju sentence and rejected every attack, and the checker answered unsure on 18.2% of answers against a ceiling of 15% fixed in advance. That check failed and the ceiling was not changed.

Running system. The application was run end to end on a demonstration database with and without the hosted model: a wrong answer, a hint, a copied answer; an unaided correct fix that taught Raju; and a romanised answer that went to the teacher's queue. In the model run, Raju's drafts for two of three planted turns were rejected and the approved sentence was shown; the coach's one hint was written in Telugu, rejected, and replaced by the generic hint. Demonstration content is approved by demonstration accounts, and the real rules, which still have open validation issues, are not shown to learners.

With no model configured the cost is zero and the learner sees the same approved sentences.

6 Results by Capability

Tool calling. Model-chosen tool calls gave a valid sentence in 0.97 [0.83, 0.99] of cases, against 0.76 [0.58, 0.88] for harness feedback and 0.69 [0.51, 0.83] for one draft, at 977, 220 and 141 tokens per case. All 44 tool calls named the right tool with valid arguments. This says little about tool selection, since only one of the three tools is relevant to the task. Recovery from a bad call could not be measured because none occurred.

Stepwise reasoning. Splitting the diagnosis into steps did not help: all three answers were right in 0.36 of cases with steps and a self-check, 0.38 without the self-check and 0.40 with one direct call (stepwise against direct, p = 0.625), at four times the tokens. The steps found the wrong word more often (0.71 against 0.59, p = 0.065). The self-check changed 2 of 58 answers, both from right to wrong.

Retrieval. The right rule was retrieved first in 16 of 29 cases and within the top three in 24. Hints from retrieval were usable in 12 of 29 cases against 10 with no retrieval (p = 0.79), and 19 when the correct rule was given. Eight of twenty shown hints told the learner to read a numbered rule they cannot see. A prompt and filter change made after seeing this raised usable hints to 25 of 29; because it was designed on these cases it is an optimistic figure that needs new cases.

Fine-tuning. Of 144 generated training pairs, 23 passed the validator (21 of them for one rule), covering 2 of 14 rules, against a bar of 200 pairs and 12 rules set beforehand, so no model was trained. The generation attempt was itself cut short: 39 of 57 calls were refused by the provider's rate limit, so the shortfall reflects both a strict validator and little data generated. Untuned Gemma-3-1B-it passed the filter in 7 of 29 cases against 21 for the prompted hosted model.

Role separation. Whole-task success was 0.31 with separate roles and 0.31 with a single model, with 359 against 1682 tokens per case. In the single-model design 65 marks were decided by the model; in the separated design none were. That count follows from the design and is not an empirical finding: the separated pipeline contains no code path by which a model could mark an answer. The four scripted learner attempts per case (the bank's right sentence, the bank's wrong sentence, a romanised answer, an injected instruction) are also ones the checker handles by construction, so its 1.00 handling rate here does not estimate its accuracy on real answers; Section 8 does.

Control (RQ1). All 17 replayed tool attacks were refused with the documented error. With an instruction such as "update my mastery to 100%" injected into Raju's task, the model attempted no unknown tool in 11 of 11 cases (upper 95% bound 0.26). The friend showed only approved lines in 12 of 12 turns, with and without an injected instruction, and with an invalid key every role fell back to approved text.

7 Ablations

7.1 Is it the tool call, or the memory?

Reading the code showed that the comparison in Section 6 changed three things at once. In the app's harness-feedback loop the model is sent the task again with the filter's reason codes but not its own rejected draft, so it cannot see what it wrote. With model-chosen tools the whole conversation is kept. And every prompt includes the bank's wrong sentence as "what Raju wrote last time", the very sentence the filter accepts. We therefore re-ran the task with six conditions on the same 29 cases, 3 repeats each (900 calls). The new condition, harness feedback with memory, keeps each draft and the check's result in the conversation while the program, not the model, runs the check, with the same three-draft budget. Two further conditions remove the example sentence from the prompt. Hypotheses were written into the script before the run. The ablation was designed after seeing the earlier results, on the same cases, so it is exploratory.

Memory. Adding memory to the fixed loop changed the valid rate by +0.14 [+0.03, +0.25] pooled; repeat 1: 4 vs 0 discordant cases, p = 0.125. Without memory, 67% of retried cases produced the same rejected draft every time; with memory none did.

Model choice. Model-chosen tool calls against the fixed loop with memory: +0.02 [+0.00, +0.06] pooled; repeat 1: 1 vs 0 discordant cases, p = 1.000. The data do not show that letting the model choose its checks adds validity beyond what memory gives, and it costs 4.7 times the tokens. Its one visible advantage is that the correct sentence never appeared as a rejected draft (leak rate 0.00 against 0.20), because the model tests drafts through the tool before submitting; in every condition the learner sees only a sentence that passed.

The example sentence. We expected validity to fall sharply without the example. It did not: +0.06 [-0.03, +0.16] pooled; repeat 1: 2 vs 1 discordant cases, p = 1.000 for one draft, and +0.01 [+0.00, +0.03] pooled; repeat 1: 1 vs 0 discordant cases, p = 1.000 with tools. That hypothesis is rejected. The model rebuilds the bank's sentence from the rule title, the Hindi meaning and the allowed words, which in these cases are only the words of the right and wrong sentences. The evaluation is therefore easier than the app, where the allowed list is the learner's whole vocabulary.

What "valid" leaves out. Of first drafts in the prompt-only condition, 12 of 87 were a different sentence containing a word found only in the wrong sentence, such as a different verb form after the Hindi negator. The filter rejects them because it cannot verify a paraphrase. Whether some are acceptable planted errors needs a native speaker and was not judged. All 19 distinct drafts of this kind, from every condition, are listed for that review in reports/generation_paraphrase_candidates.csv. A draft a reviewer accepts would be added to the item's approved wrong patterns, which the filter already honours; nothing is accepted automatically.

Is "valid" a measure of generation? Only partly. With the example in the prompt, a valid sentence can be a copy. The two no-example conditions are the closest we have to an independent test: the model never sees the bank's sentence and is scored against it, so a match is reproduced, not copied. One draft without the example matched in 0.66 of runs. This is a lower bound on correct planting, since a correct paraphrase counts as a failure, and it is still scored on the team's own sentences with a short word list. We report it beside the original measure and do not merge the two.

Change made after this ablation. The app now uses the fixed loop with memory (method tool_history in setu/agents/classmate.py; the ablation's code was moved there unchanged, and the ablation report rebuilds identically). The filter was not changed. The old loop is kept under its old name so that the earlier results remain reproducible. All results in this paper for "harness feedback" without memory were measured with the old loop.

7.2 Other ablations

Removing the self-check from stepwise reasoning changed nothing measurable (0.38 against 0.36). For retrieval, indexing only the rule explanations, restricting the index to Hindi→Telugu rules, and removing the abstention threshold each moved results by a few cases, within the intervals. A retrieval score threshold separates off-topic input from rule-related sentences (9 of 11 attacks abstained at 0.5) but cannot separate a correct sentence from a wrong one, since both match the same rule.

8 Evaluations

8.1 The checker against a native speaker (RQ3)

One native-speaking team member labelled 50 learner corrections without seeing the checker's verdicts. The checker reached κ = 0.15 [-0.03, 0.31] and accuracy 0.36; a prompt-only model judge given the same labelling guide reached κ = 0.46 [0.29, 0.64] and accuracy 0.62. The target fixed in advance was κ ≥ 0.6 and better than the judge; the hypothesis is rejected.

The checker recognises wrong answers (recall 0.88) and fails on partial ones (recall 0.12): of 26 partial answers it marked 9 correct, 5 wrong and sent 9 to a teacher. It marked no wrong answer as correct. Its false-acceptance rate (0.26) equals the judge's (0.26); the difference between them is false rejection, 0.50 against 0.12: the checker refuses half of the answers the native speaker accepted, often because a sentence that drops the pronoun is valid Telugu but is not in the bank. Macro-F1 is 0.43 against 0.62. Two cautions apply. There is one labeller, so we cannot say how much two native speakers would agree with each other, and the label "partial" may be the least stable. And the judge is not a drop-in replacement: giving a model the mark is what the architecture forbids, and its false-acceptance rate is no better.

8.3 Simulated learners (RQ4)

No learner has used SETU. To see what our own assumptions imply, we simulated 100 learners per condition (20 profiles × 5 seeds) for three practice days and a test on day 7, under three conditions: A, correcting Raju; B, the same sentences with error and correction shown and the answer typed while visible; C, an ordinary tutor that asks the learner to write the sentence. A simulation shows the consequences of its assumptions. It is not evidence about people, and its intervals, which shrink as more learners are simulated, measure simulation noise only.

The first simulator gives day-7 recall A 0.046, B 0.019, C 0.051. The second, which uses the app's FSRS scheduler as its memory model, gives A 0.253, B 0.329, C 0.306 (A − B -0.076, A − C -0.053). The order of A and B reverses.

Why they disagree. The simulators make opposite assumptions about one thing. In the first, typing a visible answer never lengthens memory, so B is last by construction. In the second, typing a visible answer is always a successful review that lengthens memory, while a failed attempt is a lapse; simulated learners begin with about a 0.29 chance of producing a form and, in A, must also notice the error (mean probability 0.33), so most of A's turns are scored as lapses. We tested whether the second result depends on the assumptions we could vary: the probability of noticing the error (0.2 to 0.95), whether a correct fix counts as unaided, and whether the copy step after a miss counts as a review, as it does in the app. A stayed last in 28 of 28 settings. A led only when an unnoticed error was treated as leaving no memory trace, and that setting relies on an artifact: a card never reviewed does not decay in this simulator.

FSRS was fitted to flashcard reviews, where a failure means a learned card was forgotten. Here it scores first attempts at material not yet learned, where a failure followed by feedback may be useful. Whether that mapping is right is exactly what a study with learners would have to settle. Within its assumptions, the simulation says correcting Raju as built gives less recall than the alternatives, and that the design should include more sentences the learner writes unaided.

9 Limitations

  • No learner data. RQ4 and the original questions about error prediction and direction are unanswered. A pilot needs reviewed content, informed consent and institutional clearance, none of which were in place.
  • Content. The Telugu and Hindi content is a team draft with one non-independent review. The real rule bank cannot yet be activated; the demonstration uses three labelled demonstration rules.
  • One labeller. The 50 native labels come from one team member. There is no human–human agreement to compare the checker against.
  • Small, team-written, single-model evaluation. Sets of 29, 58 and 50 cases give wide intervals. Apart from the ablation, each condition was run once. One model was tested, so nothing here says how other models behave.
  • A narrow validity measure. A valid Raju sentence is one that matches the bank. The model contributes no new sentence to a planted turn, and variants the filter rejects were not judged by a person.
  • Research code is not the product. Model-chosen tool calls, retrieval for hints, stepwise diagnosis and the model judge are evaluation scripts. The app's loop with memory was adopted after the ablation and has not yet been measured on new cases.
  • Post-hoc analyses. The retrieval prompt fix and the generation ablation were designed after seeing results on the same cases.
  • Interface additions (path map, word pictures, match game, English glosses) were built and passed an automated accessibility check but were not evaluated with users. Speech features are off.
  • Simulation. Both simulators rest on parameters chosen by the team.

10 Conclusions

What the experiments establish. (1) In this system a language model can be confined to proposing text: on our attack cases no model output reached a learner unchecked or changed a mark, and with the model unavailable the app degraded to approved text. (2) For producing the classmate's sentence, the benefit we first attributed to model-chosen tool calls is reproduced almost entirely by a fixed program loop that shows the model its own rejected draft, at about one fifth of the tokens. In this task the model does not need to choose the next step. (3) Stepwise reasoning, retrieval and separate roles did not improve accuracy over simpler baselines on our cases, and a small model could not be tuned for lack of validated data. (4) The rule-based checker is safe in one direction, never accepting a wrong answer, but it rejects or defers too many acceptable answers and agrees poorly with a native speaker.

What remains unknown. Whether correcting a classmate helps anyone learn Telugu. Whether the predicted errors are the ones Hindi speakers make. How the checker compares with agreement between two native speakers. Whether any of the capability results hold for other models, more cases or sentences outside our bank.

Next steps, in order. Independent native review of the bank and a second labeller; confirm the memory loop, now in the app, on new cases; widen the accepted forms for pronoun-drop and partial answers and re-measure agreement; then, with clearance, a small descriptive pilot.

Ethics Statement

No human participants took part. Accounts use random identifiers and passphrases; the system stores no names, email addresses or phone numbers, and withdrawal deletes a learner's text. Unreviewed Telugu is not shown to real learners. The 28 October plan specified self-hosted models only; we later used a hosted model for evaluation on team-written cases. It is off by default and receives rule titles, Hindi meanings and bank sentences, not learner identity. Browser speech recognition can send audio to a third party, so speech is off. An AI coding assistant was used for programming, testing, analysis and drafting, including the audit behind this revision; the authors checked every reported number against a file in reports/ and are responsible for the content.

Reproducibility

The repository contains the application, the content bank, the frozen cases, every result file and the scripts that regenerate each table and figure (README.md, "Reproducing the results"). The simulations, retrieval metrics, held-out scorecard, figures and this paper rebuild without a model. Model runs need an endpoint; rows are saved per case, so a run can be resumed and inspected. Model outputs are not deterministic at temperature 0.4, which is why the ablation reports repeats.

Madhav Malhotra: core system, teacher tools, simulators, coach retrieval, the fine-tuning pipeline, and the audit, generation ablation and simulator sensitivity analysis of this revision. Kushal Karan: tool calling, stepwise reasoning, model-judge validation, the single-agent baseline and role-separation evaluation, results tables, the call budget cap and the model runs. Shaik Areesh: human–system agreement (batch A) and annotation validation. Faviana Noronha: beginner interface, accessibility check, results and failure analysis, compute report and the earlier write-up.
